title: What Happens When You Zoom Into sin(1/x)?
originalTopic: Zoom behavior, nonexistence of a limit, and aliasing artifacts
author: Muhammad Abdullah Athar
problemStatement: Zoom repeatedly toward the origin on the graph of y = sin(1/x). Describe what happens to the number of visible oscillations, whether the curve seems to approach a single value, and why the picture at extreme zoom cannot be trusted.
finalAnswer: \text{Infinitely many oscillations in every window about } x = 0; \quad \lim_{x \to 0} \sin(1/x) \text{ does not exist}

steps.title: Locate the zeros
steps.explanation: The crossings pile up toward 0 with spacing about 1/(n*pi) which shrinks without bound.
steps.why: Explicit zeros prove the graph keeps crossing the axis no matter how far you zoom, so the zooming never stabilizes.

steps.title: Count oscillations inside a window
steps.explanation: Any interval around 0, however small, corresponds to an unbounded range of the angle 1/x, so it contains infinitely many full periods, and the peaks stay at plus or minus 1.
steps.why: Because the amplitude never shrinks while the frequency grows without bound, no single value can be the limit at 0.

steps.title: Explain the aliasing artifact
steps.explanation: A plotter evaluates only a few hundred or thousand equally spaced x-values. Once oscillations are finer than that spacing, the render collapses into a filled band, a few smooth false curves, or an apparently solid block between y = -1 and y = 1.
steps.why: Under-sampling a high-frequency signal produces aliasing, so beyond some zoom level the screen depicts the sampling grid rather than the function.

steps.title: Practical reading strategy
steps.explanation: Doubling the sample count and zooming again shows that the band between -1 and 1 is always filled, which is the honest mathematical conclusion; the specific squiggles inside it are not.
steps.why: Distinguishing stable features from sample-dependent ones is the core skill of reading computer-generated graphs critically.
